events.fact: The Pony Express began its first ride, with riders departing simultaneously from St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, to carry the mail across nearly two thousand miles of frontier.
President Harry S. Truman signed the Foreign Assistance Act, launching the Marshall Plan that sent thirteen billion dollars to rebuild a war-shattered Europe.

block: On April 3, 1860, the first riders of the Pony Express spurred out from St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, beginning a relay that would carry the mail nearly two thousand miles across mountain and desert at the cost of great hardship and faithful duty. On the same day in 1948, President Harry S. Truman signed the act that launched the Marshall Plan, pouring American treasure into the rebuilding of a Europe broken by war so that ruined nations might stand again. An Obedient citizen learns from both that a charge once accepted is to be carried through, whether the burden is a mail pouch promised to a distant town or a duty owed to a needful neighbor, for He who appoints our tasks expects them faithfully discharged.

events.fact: Congress passed the Flag Act of 1818, fixing the United States flag at thirteen stripes for the original colonies and one star for each state, with a new star added on the Fourth of July following each admission.
President William Henry Harrison died of pneumonia one month into his term, the first president to die in office, and Vice President John Tyler succeeded him in an orderly transfer of power.

block: On April 4, 1818, Congress passed the Flag Act that settled the design of the national banner at thirteen stripes for the founding colonies and a single star for every state, so that the flag might grow with the Republic yet never lose the memory of its origin. On the same day in 1841, President William Henry Harrison died of pneumonia only a month after his inauguration, the first chief magistrate to fall in office, and the young nation steadied itself as Vice President John Tyler quietly took up the burden under the rule of law. A Steadfast citizen holds his post as that constitution held, trusting that even when men fail and fall the providence of God preserves what is built upon enduring foundations.

events.fact: Pocahontas married the English planter John Rolfe at Jamestown, Virginia, a union that secured several years of peace between the colonists and the Powhatan people.
President George Washington cast the first presidential veto in American history, returning an apportionment bill he judged to violate the Constitution.

block: On April 5, 1614, Pocahontas was married to the English planter John Rolfe at Jamestown, a covenant blessed by both her father the chief and the colony's governor that bought years of peace between two peoples who might easily have destroyed one another. On the same day in 1792, President George Washington cast the first veto in the nation's history, returning an apportionment bill because he believed it broke the bounds the Constitution had set, submitting his own office to the higher law he had sworn to defend. An Obedient citizen sees in both that true peace and true authority alike are won by submission to what is right, bending the will to the limits God and conscience appoint rather than to mere desire.

events.fact: Robert Peary, with Matthew Henson and four Inuit companions, claimed to have reached the North Pole after years of grueling Arctic expeditions.
The United States entered the First World War when the House of Representatives passed the declaration of war against Germany in the early hours of the morning.

block: On April 6, 1909, after years of frostbitten failure and stubborn return to the ice, Robert Peary and Matthew Henson with four Inuit companions planted their flag at what they believed to be the North Pole, the prize of a lifetime's relentless toil. On the same day in 1917, the House of Representatives voted in the small hours to declare war on Germany, and the United States set its hand to a hard and bloody task an ocean away. A Steadfast citizen presses on as those explorers pressed across the polar waste and as those soldiers crossed the sea, enduring the long cold labor until the work appointed by God is finished.

events.fact: Pioneers of the Ohio Company under General Rufus Putnam landed at the mouth of the Muskingum River and founded Marietta, the first permanent American settlement in the Northwest Territory.
Union forces under General Ulysses S. Grant launched a counterattack on the second day of the Battle of Shiloh in Tennessee, reclaiming the lost ground and securing a hard-won victory.

block: On April 7, 1788, forty-eight men of the Ohio Company under General Rufus Putnam stepped ashore where the Muskingum joins the Ohio and raised Marietta, the first lasting American settlement in the vast Northwest Territory, planting law and labor in the wilderness. On the same day in 1862, General Ulysses S. Grant, reinforced overnight after a terrible first day, threw his army forward at Shiloh and drove the Confederates back over the blood-soaked ground they had taken, winning at fearful cost. A Steadfast citizen builds as those settlers built and stands as those soldiers stood, refusing to abandon the ground entrusted to him and trusting God to bless the work of patient, unyielding hands.

events.fact: The United States Senate passed the Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery by a vote of thirty-eight to six, sending it toward eventual ratification.
The Seventeenth Amendment was ratified when Connecticut gave the final state approval, establishing the direct election of United States senators by the people.

block: On April 8, 1864, after long and bitter debate, the United States Senate passed the Thirteenth Amendment to abolish slavery throughout the land, a great labor of conscience that would not be fully ratified for another year and more. On the same day in 1913, the Seventeenth Amendment was completed when Connecticut cast the deciding vote, giving the people the direct choice of their senators. A Steadfast citizen takes heart that the slow and costly work of perfecting self-government goes forward year upon year, and he lends his own patient hand to it, knowing that God honors those who persevere in the labor of justice and ordered liberty.

events.fact: General Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Ulysses S. Grant at Wilmer McLean's home in Appomattox Court House, effectively ending the Civil War.
American and Filipino forces on the Bataan Peninsula surrendered to the Japanese, the largest surrender in American military history, leading to the brutal Bataan Death March.

block: On April 9, 1865, General Robert E. Lee laid down his sword to General Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of the McLean house at Appomattox, and Grant's generous terms let weary men keep their horses and go home, binding up a nation's wounds even in the hour of victory. On the same day in 1942, the starving defenders of Bataan surrendered to the Japanese, and tens of thousands of loyal Americans and Filipinos passed into a death march of unspeakable cruelty, faithful to one another to the bitter end. A Loyal citizen honors the devotion of men who kept faith with their comrades and their cause through surrender and suffering alike, and he holds fast to his own bonds of duty, trusting God to vindicate every faithful sacrifice.

events.fact: President George Washington signed the Patent Act of 1790, the first United States patent law, establishing protection for inventors and the foundation of American industry.
Walter Hunt of New York received Patent No. 6,281 for the safety pin, a humble invention whose rights he sold for only four hundred dollars.

block: On April 10, 1790, President George Washington signed the first Patent Act, granting inventors the sole right to the fruit of their ingenuity and laying a cornerstone for the honest industry that would build a continent. On the same day in 1849, the New York mechanic Walter Hunt twisted a length of wire into the safety pin and earned Patent No. 6,281, though he parted with the rights for a mere four hundred dollars and never grew rich from it. A Steadfast citizen labors as these men labored, content to do good and useful work with his hands whether or not the reward is great, trusting that God sees the faithful toil that men overlook.

events.fact: Confederate batteries opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning the American Civil War.
Dr. Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe and effective at the University of Michigan, ending the terror of an epidemic that had crippled thousands of children.

block: On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, and the long-feared war between the states began amid the smoke over the water. On the same day in 1955, scientists at the University of Michigan announced that Dr. Jonas Salk's vaccine against polio was safe and effective, and across the land church bells rang and parents wept for joy as a terror that had crippled their children was at last broken. An Obedient citizen remembers that nations reap what they sow, and he submits himself to the labor of healing and peace rather than the works of strife, seeking with Salk's patient diligence to be a mender and not a destroyer under the hand of God.

events.fact: Thomas Jefferson, principal author of the Declaration of Independence and third president, was born at Shadwell in the colony of Virginia.
Major Robert Anderson surrendered Fort Sumter after a thirty-four-hour bombardment, with not a single man killed in the opening battle of the Civil War.

block: On April 13, 1743, Thomas Jefferson was born at Shadwell in Virginia, the man whose pen would frame the self-evident truths that all are created equal and endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights. On the same day in 1861, Major Robert Anderson struck his colors at Fort Sumter after a day and a half of bombardment, surrendering the fort yet, by God's mercy, having lost not one man in the war's first exchange. An Obedient citizen treasures the truths Jefferson confessed and submits to the lawful order they uphold, knowing that the rights of men rest not on human whim but on the will of the God who made them.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln was shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre in Washington, days after the Civil War's effective end.
The RMS Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic late at night on her maiden voyage and began to sink, drowning more than fifteen hundred souls.

block: On the night of April 14, 1865, just as the guns of the Civil War fell silent, John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, and the man who had labored to bind up the nation lay mortally wounded. On the same night in 1912, the great liner Titanic, thought unsinkable by her builders, struck an iceberg in the dark Atlantic and began her descent that would carry more than fifteen hundred to the deep. An Obedient citizen is sobered by both, remembering that the pride of men and the malice of men alike are humbled in an hour, and that the wise submit their days to God, who alone holds life and death in His hand.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln died at the Petersen House at 7:22 in the morning, the first American president to be assassinated.
The RMS Titanic sank in the North Atlantic at 2:20 in the morning, claiming more than fifteen hundred lives in one of history's deadliest peacetime maritime disasters.

block: On the morning of April 15, 1865, President Abraham Lincoln breathed his last in the Petersen House across from Ford's Theatre, the first president felled by an assassin, and a grieving nation laid down its rejoicing for mourning. On the same morning in 1912, the Titanic slipped beneath the freezing Atlantic, and the boast that no power could sink her was answered by the deep that swallowed more than fifteen hundred souls. An Obedient citizen bows before the sovereignty of God in these dark hours, confessing that no greatness of station nor work of human hands can stand against His will, and ordering his own life in humble submission while it is yet day.

events.fact: George Washington departed his beloved Mount Vernon to journey to New York for his inauguration as the first president of the United States.
Wilbur Wright, who with his brother Orville achieved the first powered flight, was born near Millville, Indiana.

block: On April 16, 1789, George Washington bade adieu to Mount Vernon and to private life, setting out for New York with, as he wrote, a mind oppressed with painful sensations, yet going because his country called him to the presidency. On the same day in 1867, Wilbur Wright was born near Millville, Indiana, the elder of two bicycle-makers who would conquer the air itself through years of patient, scientific labor. A Steadfast citizen answers the call of duty as Washington did though it cost him his ease, and toils as the Wrights toiled though the goal seems impossible, trusting God to honor the faithful endurance of His servants.

events.fact: The explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing for France, became the first European to enter New York Harbor and describe its waters.
Brigade 2506, a force of Cuban exiles backed by the United States, landed at the Bay of Pigs in a failed attempt to overthrow Fidel Castro's communist regime.

block: On April 17, 1524, the navigator Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed his ship Dauphine into the great harbor of New York, the first European to look upon those waters and set them down for the world to know. On the same day in 1961, some fourteen hundred Cuban exiles of Brigade 2506 landed at the Bay of Pigs to free their homeland from communist tyranny, and within three days the venture collapsed in defeat and capture. A Steadfast citizen presses into hard and uncertain endeavors as the explorer did into unknown seas, and honors the courage of men who hazarded all for liberty even when the cause failed, knowing the outcome rests at last with God and not with us alone.

events.fact: Paul Revere and other riders set out from Boston to warn the countryside that British regulars were marching, on the eve of the battles of Lexington and Concord.
A great earthquake and the fires that followed devastated San Francisco, destroying most of the city and killing more than three thousand people.

block: On the night of April 18, 1775, Paul Revere and his fellow riders galloped out of Boston to rouse the sleeping countryside, crying that the regulars were coming, so that the minutemen might stand ready at dawn. On the same day in 1906, a tremendous earthquake shook San Francisco before sunrise, and the fires that swept the broken city laid more than four-fifths of it in ashes and took over three thousand lives. A Steadfast citizen keeps watch and gives warning as Revere did through the dark, and stands firm amid sudden ruin as that stricken city's people rebuilt from the ashes, knowing that the man who trusts in God is not shaken when the earth itself trembles.

events.fact: The battles of Lexington and Concord opened the American Revolution, where colonial militia fired the 'shot heard round the world' against British troops.
A truck bomb destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, killing one hundred sixty-eight people in the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in American history.

block: On April 19, 1775, colonial militiamen stood against the British regulars on Lexington green and at Concord's North Bridge, and the shot heard round the world began the long fight for American independence. On the same day in 1995, a hateful man destroyed the federal building in Oklahoma City with a truck bomb, murdering one hundred sixty-eight people, among them little children, in the worst act of homegrown terror the nation has known. An Obedient citizen reveres the lawful liberty those farmers won and recoils from the lawless rage that razed Oklahoma City, resolving to submit his strength to righteousness and order, and entrusting the slain and the grieving to the God who judges all evil.

events.fact: President Andrew Jackson signed the law creating the Hot Springs Reservation in Arkansas, the first federal land set aside for protection, foreshadowing the national parks.
Colonel Robert E. Lee resigned his commission in the United States Army after his native Virginia seceded, declining command of the Union forces.

block: On April 20, 1832, President Andrew Jackson signed the act that reserved the Hot Springs of Arkansas as federal land, the first ground in the Republic set apart and protected for the common good, a seed of the great national parks to come. On the same day in 1861, Colonel Robert E. Lee, having declined command of the Union armies, resigned his commission with a heavy heart when Virginia left the Union, choosing the painful path his conscience demanded. A Steadfast citizen guards what is entrusted to him as that reserved land was guarded, and respects the weight of a hard decision faithfully made, knowing that God calls every man to stand where conviction and duty place him whatever the cost.

events.fact: The Oklahoma Land Rush opened the Unassigned Lands at high noon, when some fifty thousand settlers raced to claim nearly two million acres of homestead land.
Congress passed the Coinage Act of 1864 authorizing the two-cent piece, the first United States coin to bear the motto 'In God We Trust.'

block: On April 22, 1889, at the crack of a gun at high noon, tens of thousands of settlers surged into the Unassigned Lands of Oklahoma to stake their homesteads, and by nightfall whole cities had risen from the empty prairie through the sweat of eager hands. On the same day in 1864, in the dark middle of the Civil War, Congress passed the Coinage Act that placed upon the new two-cent piece the words 'In God We Trust,' the first time that confession appeared on American coin. A Steadfast citizen labors to build as those homesteaders built and openly owns his trust in the Almighty as that humble coin proclaimed, planting his hope not in the works of his hands alone but in the God whose name he is unashamed to bear.

events.fact: Boston Latin School was founded in Massachusetts, the first public school in what would become the United States, educating five future signers of the Declaration of Independence.
George Washington arrived in New York City to triumphal welcome, a week before taking the oath as the first president of the United States.

block: On April 23, 1635, the people of Boston founded Boston Latin School, the first public school in the land, where Puritan masters trained boys in the classics and conscience, and from whose benches would come five signers of the Declaration of Independence. On the same day in 1789, George Washington reached New York to the cheers of a grateful people, having left his farm at his country's call to take up the presidency a week later. A Loyal citizen treasures the faithful institutions that form a free people and the devoted servants who answer when duty calls, giving himself as Washington gave himself, in steadfast allegiance to his country and his God.

events.fact: President John Adams signed the act establishing the Library of Congress, appropriating funds for the books and the room to house the young nation's library.
The Hubble Space Telescope was carried into orbit aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery, opening an unmatched window upon the heavens.

block: On April 24, 1800, President John Adams signed the act that founded the Library of Congress, setting aside money for the books a wise legislature would need, planting a great storehouse of knowledge for the Republic. On the same day in 1990, the Space Shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit, where it would gaze farther into the heavens than any eye before it. A Steadfast citizen builds patiently for those who come after, gathering wisdom as Adams gathered books and reaching upward as Hubble reached toward the stars, for the heavens declare the glory of God, and the diligent labor of one generation lights the way for the next.

events.fact: John James Audubon, the great naturalist and painter of 'The Birds of America,' was born at Les Cayes in the West Indies and later made his life and work in America.
John Wilkes Booth, the assassin of President Lincoln, was cornered in a Virginia tobacco barn and killed, ending the great manhunt twelve days after the murder.

block: On April 26, 1785, John James Audubon was born in the West Indies, and in the forests and rivers of his adopted America he would spend a lifetime studying and painting the birds, leaving the magnificent plates of 'The Birds of America' as a hymn to creation. On the same day in 1865, Union cavalry cornered the assassin John Wilkes Booth in a Virginia barn, and there he met his end twelve days after he had murdered the president, justice overtaking him at last. A Steadfast citizen devotes his days to faithful and worthy work as Audubon devoted his to creation's beauty, confident that the patient labors of righteous men endure while the schemes of the wicked are brought to nothing under the just hand of God.

events.fact: Maryland ratified the United States Constitution by a vote of sixty-three to eleven, becoming the seventh state to join the new federal union.
James Monroe, fifth president and author of the Monroe Doctrine, was born in Westmoreland County, Virginia; he left college to fight in the Revolution and was wounded at Trenton.

block: On April 28, 1788, the convention of Maryland ratified the United States Constitution by a decisive vote, making her the seventh state to bind herself to the new federal compact and submit to its lawful order. On the same day in 1758, James Monroe was born in Westmoreland County, Virginia, a man who as a youth laid down his studies to take up arms with Washington and was wounded crossing the Delaware at Trenton before rising to the presidency. An Obedient citizen submits himself gladly to rightful authority as Maryland submitted to the Constitution, and answers the call of duty as young Monroe answered it, yielding his own will to the ordered service that God appoints for a free people.

events.fact: New Orleans surrendered to Union forces after Flag Officer David Farragut's fleet ran past the Confederate forts and seized the South's largest port.
American soldiers of the 42nd, 45th, and 20th divisions liberated the Dachau concentration camp, freeing some thirty-two thousand prisoners from Nazi captivity.

block: On April 29, 1862, the city of New Orleans surrendered after Flag Officer David Farragut had driven his fleet upriver past the blazing guns of two Confederate forts, wresting the Confederacy's greatest port from its grasp. On the same day in 1945, American soldiers broke open the gates of the Dachau concentration camp and freed some thirty-two thousand wasted prisoners, looking upon horrors that hardened their resolve against tyranny forever. A Steadfast citizen stands firm against evil as Farragut stood firm under fire and as those soldiers stood against the cruelty of Dachau, enduring danger and dread to set captives free, for the God of justice strengthens the hands that fight for the oppressed.

events.fact: George Washington was inaugurated as the first president of the United States on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York, taking the oath upon a Bible and kissing it.
American envoys signed the Louisiana Purchase treaty in Paris, buying some 828,000 square miles from France and doubling the size of the United States.

block: On April 30, 1789, George Washington stood on the balcony of Federal Hall and took the first presidential oath with his hand upon the Scriptures, kissing the Bible before the cheering crowd as cannon thundered and a new nation entrusted itself to his leadership and to Providence. On the same day in 1803, American envoys in Paris signed the treaty for the Louisiana Purchase, buying an empire of land from France and doubling the Republic at a stroke. A Steadfast citizen reveres the solemn beginning Washington gave the nation upon God's Word and the vast inheritance secured that same day, holding fast to both the faith and the freedom handed down to him, and guarding them faithfully for the generations to come.
